title: Nonlinear programming via an exact penalty function: asymptotic analysis
contribution: Proves local convergence and a 2-step superlinear rate for the local phase of the Coleman-Conn exact-penalty method, obtained by removing the Z^T B v term from the RQP step and restoring with constraint values re-evaluated at x+h; also shows by construction that the RQP direction can increase the exact penalty at points arbitrarily close to x*. (Read from the Waterloo report CS-80-30, June 1980, via page images; the text file is empty.)
problem_entry: RQP is fast locally but not robustly global, and no globalization is yet satisfactory; the authors' own global exact-penalty method [4] has numbers and a global proof, and this paper is meant to prove its superlinear rate and compare it with RQP; a geometric reading of the RQP step reveals unnecessary computation and storage (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Split the RQP step into a vertical step v (Newton on the active constraints, exact information) and a horizontal step h (approximate projected Newton step); following Powell, drop the Z^T B v term, take h first and v after it with constraint values re-evaluated at x+h, so that only the projected Hessian is needed and no refactorization occurs; this is exactly what the global method reduces to near x* (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: f and phi_i C^2, second-order sufficiency, iterates in a compact W, linearly independent active gradients, active set identified, uniform bounds on Z^T B Z, x_k -> x*, and for the rate Z^T B Z -> Z*^T G_L Z*, which is admitted to require gradient differencing near x* (pp. 5, 8-9, 11, 15).
proof_devices: orthogonal error split x - x* = A w + Z u with a separable 2-step superlinear criterion (Lemma 4, p. 10)
tangential step changes constraint values only at O(||h||^2), giving ||v|| <= L2||x - x*|| (Lemma 2, p. 9)
mean-value form phi_j(x_k) = grad phi_j(xi_j)^T (x_k - x*) with an error matrix E_k -> 0 (Theorem 1, pp. 10-11)
2-step contraction: 1/4 bounds on each error component give ||x^2 - x*|| <= 1/2 ||x^0 - x*|| (Lemmas 5-6, Theorem 4, pp. 12-13)
local counterexample for RQP: p(x'+d) - p(x') = -1/2 d^T[G_f + sum(1/mu - 2 lambda_i)G_phi_i]d + o(||d||^2), negative definite bracket for lambda_i in (0, 1/(2mu)) (pp. 14-15)
experiments: none in this paper; numerical results are in the companion global-analysis report [4], whose implementation uses rank-2 updates far from x* and switches to gradient differencing near it (pp. 4, 15).
positioning: Continues the authors' own [3], [4] and the Conn-Pietrzykowski penalty line [7]; uses Powell [15] as setting and tool; credits Murray-Wright; criticizes Han directly: global and superlinear properties do not mesh without an unsafe switch (pp. 4-7, 14, 16).
writing: 12 printed pages; the algorithm is derived from a geometric reading of the rival's step; lettered assumptions; a one-word proof of the combination lemma; the conclusion is a question about the rival answered by construction; one slip (a reference to an Algorithm 2 that does not appear) (pp. 4-15).
limits_future: The rate needs projected-Hessian convergence, which needs expensive differencing near x*; future work: a full quasi-Newton version, justified by Powell's result that accuracy along the search directions suffices; delivered in S021 (p. 15).

method_links.note: The triad is split over two reports: global analysis with numbers in [4], local theory here. The theorem is tied to the code by the global-to-local reduction, and the implementation's switch to gradient differencing is what satisfies Theorem 2's hypothesis. This paper itself has no code or numbers.
Conn's exact penalty (1977 line) is combined with the RQP school's fast local step, and Powell's RQP result is reused as a proof tool.
Weak evidence: constraint-manifold structure is used so that only the projected Hessian is approximated and A is not refactorized.

Precursor: the rate is carried by an explicit model-accuracy condition (projected-Hessian convergence) that the code enforces by switching to finite differences near x*; it concerns Hessian accuracy, not geometry.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The global exact-penalty method automatically reduces to Algorithm 1 near a solution, so only the simple local algorithm is analysed for the rate.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: counterexample against the rival in the conclusion
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: By construction, the RQP direction can increase the exact penalty arbitrarily close to x*, even in convex examples.
Future work names a full quasi-Newton version and the Powell result supporting it; S021 (1984) delivers it as a direct extension.
The 2-step superlinear rate is proved assuming x_k -> x* (Theorems 1-3); local convergence is proved afterwards (Lemmas 5-6, Theorem 4).

transferable: Write the competitor's step as range-space plus null-space parts, sort the terms by exact vs approximate information, and drop the term the theory says is unimportant (pp. 5-7).
Prove 2-step superlinear convergence separably: a one-step rate on the range component and a two-step rate on the null component (Lemma 4, p. 10).
Prove local convergence by 2-step contraction: 1/4 bounds on each component give 1/2 overall, and a linear bound handles the odd iterates (pp. 12-13).
Build a local negative result for a rival by expanding your merit function along its step and choosing multipliers that make the quadratic form negative definite (pp. 14-15).
End with a future-work paragraph that names the next theorem and the published result that makes it plausible (p. 15).

title: On the local convergence of a quasi-Newton method for the nonlinear programming problem
contribution: A local quasi-Newton method for equality-constrained nonlinear programming that recurs a positive-definite approximation to the projected Lagrangian Hessian by a projected DFP/BFGS update, proved locally 2-step Q-superlinearly convergent without convexity. (Read from the Cornell report TR 82-509, August 1982, via page images; the text file is empty.)
problem_entry: DFP/BFGS are Q-superlinear and positive definite in the unconstrained case, but no truly Q-superlinear quasi-Newton method is known for nonconvex constrained problems; Powell (R-superlinear only), Han (convex only), Boggs-Tolle-Wang (conditions without an update) and Tanabe (no theory) each leave a gap; earlier methods keep a full n x n positive-definite matrix although only the projection must be positive definite (pp. 5-6).
key_idea: Update an (n-t)x(n-t) SPD matrix B approximating Z*^T grad^2 L Z* from reduced secant pairs built from the horizontal step (s = Z^T(x+ - x), y = Z^T[(grad f(x+) - C(x+)lambda) - grad f]); restore with v = -C(C^T C)^{-1} c(x+h); a direct extension of the Coleman-Conn local Newton method (pp. 6-7, 13).
assumptions: Equality constraints; f and c C^2 on an open convex D; singular values of C bounded above and below; Lipschitz orthonormal null-space basis Z(x); second-order sufficiency; Lipschitz Hessians on a small D; no finite convergence; x^0 near x* and B_0 near H* in the weighted norm; no convexity (pp. 8-10, 24, 26).
proof_devices: algorithm-independent sufficient condition: ||r_L|| + ||r_c|| = o(||Z^T grad f|| + ||c||) implies 2-step Q-superlinear (Theorem 2.1, p. 10)
range/null error split with a four-term T1-T4 bound on the null component (pp. 10-12)

verify the bounded-deterioration hypothesis ||My - M^{-1}s|| <= 1/3 ||M^{-1}s||, M = H*^{-1/2} (Lemma 3.3, pp. 15-16), then apply Dennis-More Lemma 3.1 in the weighted Frobenius norm ||MQM||_F (pp. 16-17)
Dennis-More-type condition along the steps under summability sum ||x_k - x*|| < infinity (Theorem 3.5, pp. 17-18)
2-step contraction: quadratic range component (Lemma 3.11) and a 1/4 null-component bound give ||x^{k+1} - x*|| <= 1/2 ||x^{k-1} - x*|| (pp. 21-23)
induction with the Banach perturbation lemma keeping ||B_k^{-1}|| <= 2 gamma and a geometric sum of deterioration increments (Theorem 3.14, pp. 24-25)
experiments: none; the practical performance is declared unknown (p. 26).
positioning: Extends the authors' 1982a,b papers; places Powell, Han, Boggs-Tolle-Wang and Tanabe by precise gap statements; credits Gill-Murray for linear constraints; openly borrows the Broyden-Dennis-More and Dennis-More machinery; claims conditions slightly more general than Powell's (pp. 5-7, 12, 16-17, 23).
writing: The abstract names the pivotal feature (projection, in bold); a roadmap; standing assumptions in bold; the diagnosis flagged as opinion; a design choice whose justification is unproven is disclosed; borrowed proofs are labelled; a half-page conclusion with open problems; about 19 pages of theory, no numbers (pp. 3, 6-10, 16-17, 23, 26).
limits_future: Local only; 2-step rather than 1-step; no numerical experience; unknown how to update projected approximations when the active set changes; penalty decrease unproven for quasi-Newton B; future: implementation, practical tests, a line search and globalization (pp. 7, 26).

method_links.note: Partial contradiction: a theorem-only paper whose practical performance is declared unknown, against the Research Taste claim that a theorem with no code and no numbers never occurs in the confirmed record; the triad is typical of the CGT period, not of the early Coleman-Conn period.
Step 1 and Taste mark 2: Theorem 2.1 is an algorithm-independent sufficient condition covering a class of methods.
The unconstrained Dennis-More / Broyden-Dennis-More quasi-Newton theory is transplanted into the null space of a constrained problem.
Exploits the fact that only the projected Hessian must be positive definite, so a smaller matrix is approximated.
The rate is carried by a model-accuracy condition along the steps (3.11), obtained from bounded deterioration; this weakens S018's requirement that the whole projected Hessian converge.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: An algorithm-independent sufficient condition on step residuals (Theorem 2.1), then a separate verification for the specific method (Lemma 3.6).
This paper is the quasi-Newton version announced in S018's future work, presented as a direct extension of Coleman-Conn 1982a,b.
Theorem 3.7 (rate, assuming summability and a linear bound) precedes the local-convergence results (Theorems 3.14-3.15).

transferable: State the rate result as an algorithm-independent condition on the residuals of the step equations, then verify it for your method in a separate lemma (pp. 10, 18-19).
To reuse Dennis-More bounded deterioration in a new setting, prove the single hypothesis it needs for your secant pair (Lemma 3.3, pp. 15-16).
Prove local convergence by induction, keeping ||B_k - H*||_M <= 2 Delta and ||B_k^{-1}|| <= 2 gamma via the Banach perturbation lemma, with geometrically summable increments (pp. 24-25).
Build the secant pair in reduced coordinates from the tangential step, with a multiplier-shifted gradient difference (p. 13).
Build the gap statement as a list of prior methods, each paired with the exact property it lacks (pp. 5-6).
If a design choice is motivated by a property proven only in a simpler case, say so, and state that the theorems also hold without the choice (p. 7).

title: Global convergence of a class of trust region algorithms for optimization with simple bounds
contribution: Extends unconstrained trust-region global convergence theory to bound-constrained nonconvex problems by generalizing the Cauchy point to the projected gradient path, under the weakest Hessian-growth condition, and proves finite active-set identification under strict complementarity and second-order convergence results.
problem_entry: Bound constraints are among the most common in practice and carry a combinatorial active-set part; Bertsekas's projection method has theory only for convex problems, while trust regions give global convergence on nonconvex unconstrained problems; the paper merges the two (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Any feasible step that achieves a fixed fraction of the model decrease at the generalized Cauchy point (the first minimizer along P[x - t w] inside the trust region) and stays in an enlarged trust region is admissible; there is no quasi-Newton-step requirement, and diagonal scaling allows preconditioned CG (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: A graded ladder: AS.1 compact feasible level set; AS.2 f C^2; AS.3 diagonal scalings with bounded inverses; AS.4 sum 1/b_k = infinity (the weakest possible, by Powell's example); AS.5-AS.6 for a true limit; AS.7 plus (155) for active-set identification; AS.8-AS.10 for second order; the algorithm is openly theoretical (pp. 2, 5-7, 17, 19, 25).
proof_devices: piecewise-quadratic slope bound between breakpoints, dq/dt <= -alpha^2 + 2t c2^2 ||B|| (Lemma 4, eq. 75, p. 11)
bound-constrained Cauchy decrease f - m >= 1/2 c3 h^2 min(h^2/b_k, Delta_k) with criticality h_k = ||P[x_k - w_k] - x_k|| (eq. 79, p. 11; eq. 29, p. 6)
minimal-counterexample radius bound Delta_k >= c4/b_k (Lemma 7, pp. 14-15)
counting argument J1 = {k <= pS(k)}, J2 = {k > pS(k)} showing sum 1/b_k < infinity, contradicting AS.4 (Theorem 8, pp. 15-16)
finite active-set identification via connected sets of limit points and bound persistence (Lemmas 12-13, Theorem 14, pp. 20-22)
Rayleigh-quotient model-accuracy condition for a second-order limit point (Theorem 17, pp. 25-27)
experiments: none here; preliminary numerical results are reported in the companion paper [5] (S011) (p. 2).
positioning: Builds on Bertsekas (bounds), More (trust-region framework) and Powell (weak Hessian condition); says its proof of the first result differs from Powell's; contrasts with Gay on cost per step; praises a Harwell bound-constrained code as efficient but lacking theory (pp. 2, 7, 14, 27).
writing: Figures for the GCP and h_k; a comment after every assumption; warns against reading lim inf as convergence and says the second-order point need not be a minimizer; a list-style conclusion ('interesting for several reasons'); light, attributed hedging (pp. 3, 6, 16, 27).
limits_future: A theoretical algorithm with no stopping rule; a true limit needs AS.5-AS.6; a_k is discontinuous; second-order results do not ensure minimizers; future: linear and nonlinear constraints, large-scale use with partial separability (pp. 5, 17, 19, 27-28).

method_links.note: Theory/testing twin with S011, cross-cited ('reported elsewhere [5]'), submitted six months apart and published in the same month.
Step 1 and Taste mark 2: the theorem covers a class (any step with a fraction of the GCP decrease; free B_k under AS.4; free scaling under AS.3).
Unconstrained trust-region theory (More, Powell) transplanted to bounds and merged with Bertsekas's projection.
Bounds handled exactly by projection, feasible iterates for hard constraints, structure-preserving diagonal scalings, partial separability for large problems.
Precursor: the theorem is carried by a checkable certificate (a fraction of the GCP decrease) that the code enforces; it certifies the step, not the model, which stays almost free under AS.4.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A cheap reference step whose decrease every admissible step must match up to a constant; all of the convergence theory rests on that inequality.
AS.1-AS.10 are introduced one result at a time, each only where a stronger conclusion needs it.

transferable: Define the generalized Cauchy point as the first model minimizer along the projected scaled-gradient path in the trust region, and accept any feasible step with a fixed fraction of its decrease (pp. 3-4).
Justify a weak condition as the weakest possible by citing the counterexample that breaks any weaker one, and list which common updates satisfy it (p. 7).
Minimal-counterexample radius bound: take the first iteration where radius x curvature falls below a threshold and show the previous iteration was very successful (Lemma 7, pp. 14-15).
Counting argument for sum 1/b_k: split iterations by k <= pS(k), bounding one part by monotonicity and the other by a geometric radius bound (pp. 15-16).
Use the projected-step length h_k = ||P[x_k - w_k] - x_k|| as the criticality measure, and draw it (p. 6).
Prove finite active-set identification under strict complementarity, then import the unconstrained rate theory unchanged (pp. 19-22).
coauthors: N. I. M. Gould, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: This last result is important because it shows that, under very mild conditions, the asymptotic behaviour of the algorithm is that of a purely unconstrained method, restricted to the subspace of variables that are not at their bounds at the solution.
This extension is obtained by generalizing the now classical notion of a Cauchy point in what seems to us a natural way.

title: Testing a class of methods for solving minimization problems with simple bounds on the variables
contribution: Implements the S008 class as GCP-by-breakpoint-recurrence plus truncated CG, tests five Hessian options on 25 problems in unconstrained and constrained forms against NAG line-search codes, and finds that exact Hessians are best and that SR1, not BFGS, is the best update inside a trust region.
problem_entry: The testing companion of the theory paper, meant to 'demonstrate the viability' of the analysed class; active-set methods change the active set slowly, bent-line-search theory covers convex problems only, and there is no experience with SQP-type subproblem methods (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: An l_inf box trust region intersected with the bounds; a GCP redefined to continue along the trust-region boundary (checked to be covered by the theory); breakpoint recurrences needing one sparse mat-vec per breakpoint; CG on the free variables stopped at a bound; a growth safeguard ||B_k|| <= c1 + k c2; no line search (pp. 3, 5-8).
assumptions: f smooth; strict complementarity for active-set identification (violated on purpose in the DEGEN problems); well-scaled problems; skip thresholds 1e-8 and 1e8 arbitrary in theory but meant to reflect problem scaling in practice (pp. 2, 5, 11, 22).
proof_devices: no new proofs: algorithmic deviations (a new GCP definition, CG restarts that enlarge the active set) are checked to stay inside the S008 theory (pp. 5, 19-20)
an explicit unproven conjecture on why SR1 wins: trust regions need model accuracy on a larger subspace than the Newton direction (p. 20)
experiments: 25 problems (23 families, n = 8-45, generalized from More-Garbow-Hillstrom, Hock-Schittkowski and Toint), each run in U (box) and C (bounds around the U solution) form, plus degenerate variants; 5 Hessian options (exact, BFGS, DFP, PSB, SR1); reports it (= f evals), de (= gradient evals), cg, gradient norm, cas, usk and time; failures marked; ratio-to-exact and rank-count tables; NAG E04LAF/KAF baselines compared on function and gradient calls; the DEGENSING failure diagnosed and rerun with CG restarts (pp. 10-23).
positioning: The testing twin of the authors' theory [3]; uses More, Steihaug and Toint; credits Brayton-Cullum for SR1 in a line search; challenges the line-search wisdom that BFGS is the best update; baseline from the rival active-set/line-search school (NAG) (pp. 3, 6, 12, 20, 22-23).
writing: Modest abstract ('The results are encouraging'); surprises flagged as such; the explanation labelled a conjecture with its difficulty stated; explicit recommendations and a research programme at the end; tables take 10 of 32 journal pages (pp. 2-3, 13-24).
limits_future: Small dense problems only; prototype timings; no theory for SR1's advantage; degeneracy slows convergence; future: large-scale problems via partial separability and preconditioning, then general nonlinear programming via augmented-Lagrangian bound-constrained subproblems (the LANCELOT plan) (pp. 3, 11-12, 20, 23-24).

method_links.note: Strong: its stated purpose is to test the analysed class; deviations are checked against the theory; a failure is fixed within what the theory allows (Table 5.10); it ends with the next theory-and-code programme.
Cost unit of function and gradient calls; every option reported in full; failures flagged and counted; baseline from the competing school (NAG line-search, active-set codes).
Pre-CUTE: the collection is built by generalizing classic small problems to n variables and generating constrained and degenerate variants; no noise tier and no application tier.
Exact second derivatives recommended whenever available; partial separability planned for large scale.
Trust region combined with truncated CG (Steihaug/Toint) and Bertsekas-style projection; SR1 carried from line-search use (Brayton-Cullum) into a trust region.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: anomaly harvested as an explicit conjecture
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: SR1's unexplained advantage and its accurate free-variable Hessian approximations are written up as an open question, which S010 (1991) later proves; the origin of c01's anomaly-driven-theory candidate.
Constrained variants from bounds x*_i + 0.1 <= x_i <= x*_i + 1.1 on odd i around the unconstrained solution, and degenerate variants that break strict complementarity on purpose.

transferable: Generate constrained test variants from an unconstrained problem with bounds x*_i + 0.1 <= x_i <= x*_i + 1.1 on odd i, starting from the projection of the original start (p. 11).
Add variants that deliberately violate one theoretical assumption (strict complementarity) to show where the theory's promises end (appendix pp. 24-25; p. 12).
Vary one design factor only, report every variant fully, and summarize with ratios to the ideal variant and rank counts, with failures counted separately (pp. 10, 12, 18-19).
Report diagnostics tied to the theory's claims: the last iteration at which the active set changed, and the number of skipped updates (p. 11).
When a failure traces to a violated assumption, rerun with a fix the theory permits and publish that table (Table 5.10, pp. 19-20, 22).
Compare with library codes on function and gradient calls, and state wins as counts out of the total (pp. 22-23).
Present an observed but unproven mechanism as an explicit open conjecture, with a reason why it is hard (p. 20).
coauthors: N. I. M. Gould, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: We believe that the important figures in such a comparison are the number of function and gradient calls required to solve the problem.
Moreover, they indicate that updating schemes which are held in good repute for line-search based methods are not necessarily the best within a trust-region context.
